name: Menachem
source_summary: King of Israel who seized the throne by assassinating the usurper Shallum, brutally sacked the city of Tiphsah when it resisted him, reigned ten years while continuing the idolatrous ways of Jeroboam, and paid heavy tribute to the Assyrian king Pul (Tiglath-pileser III), taxing wealthy Israelites to fund it.
family_friendly_summary: Menahem was a king of Israel during a violent period when the northern kingdom had many kings who took the throne by force. He killed King Shallum, who had himself only recently taken power, and became king in his place. Menahem also attacked a city called Tiphsah that would not accept his rule, an act described in the Bible as very harsh. Like the kings before him, Menahem led Israel to worship false gods instead of the true God. During his reign, a powerful foreign king named Pul threatened Israel, so Menahem paid him a huge amount of silver to keep peace, collecting the money by taxing Israel's wealthiest citizens.
adult_story: Menahem, son of Gadi, seized the throne of Israel by force, marching from Tirzah to Samaria and striking down Shallum, who had himself murdered his way to the throne only a month earlier (2 Kings 15:10, 14). Scripture records a specific and disturbing act of Menahem's violence: when the city of Tiphsah refused to open its gates to him, he attacked it, struck down its inhabitants, and 'ripped up all its women who were with child' (15:16) -- an atrocity recorded without commentary but consistent with the brutality of this era's power struggles in Israel. Menahem reigned ten years in Samaria and, like every king of the northern kingdom before him, 'did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel sin' (15:18). During his reign, Pul (the Assyrian king better known as Tiglath-pileser III) invaded the land; rather than resist, Menahem paid him a thousand talents of silver 'so that he might help him confirm his hold on the kingdom' (15:19). To raise the tribute, Menahem exacted fifty shekels of silver from every wealthy man in Israel (15:20) -- a pragmatic but costly submission that foreshadowed Israel's eventual subjugation and exile at Assyrian hands under his successors. He was succeeded by his son Pekahiah, who was assassinated within two years (15:22-25).
christ_connections: Menahem's violent seizure of a throne already built on violence illustrates the chaos and moral collapse of a kingdom that had abandoned covenant faithfulness -- a contrast with Christ, the rightful King who takes no throne by bloodshed but by righteous inheritance (Luke 1:32-33).
